title: What ended the dinosaurs
core: An asteroid impact was the main cause of the end-Cretaceous mass extinction. Whether Deccan volcanism had already weakened ecosystems, and so made the blow worse, is still contested.
status: Example map. Illustrates the format; the grades are a reasonable reading of the literature, not a scientific verdict.

nodes.label: An asteroid impact ended the dinosaurs
nodes.text: Possibly made worse by volcanism that had already weakened ecosystems.

nodes.label: Chicxulub impact
for: A layer enriched in iridium, rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids, sits at the boundary at sites worldwide (Alvarez et al., 1980).
Shocked quartz and glass spherules in the same layer, which form only under impact pressures.
The Chicxulub crater, about 180 km wide, is dated to within tens of thousands of years of the boundary.
against: Large eruptions can also bring iridium up from the mantle, so the layer alone does not rule out volcanism.
nodes.falsifier: Precise dating that puts the extinction clearly before or after the impact, rather than at it.

nodes.label: Years of darkness and cold
for: Soot from wildfires is found in boundary clay.
Climate models of the aerosol release give years of darkness and several degrees of cooling.
against: Estimates of how much soot and sulfur reached the upper atmosphere vary several-fold, and so does the length of the darkness.
nodes.falsifier: Boundary sediments showing too little soot and sulfur to darken the sky for more than a few months.

nodes.label: Food webs collapse
for: Marine plankton, and the animals that fed on them, were hit hardest.
Survivors were mostly small animals living on detritus, seeds or in fresh water, none of which need fresh plant growth.

nodes.label: Deccan Traps eruptions
for: One of the largest volcanic episodes in Earth's history, with pulses dated to the last few hundred thousand years of the Cretaceous.
against: Two leading dating studies (2019) disagree on whether the largest pulses came before or after the impact.

nodes.label: Ecosystems already weakened
for: Some records show a few degrees of warming in the last few hundred thousand years before the boundary.
Two other mass extinctions, end-Permian and end-Triassic, line up with eruptions of the same kind (the Siberian Traps and the Central Atlantic province).
against: Many fossil records show no decline before the boundary.
Sparse fossils make a sudden extinction look gradual (the Signor-Lipps effect), so apparent early declines can be an artefact.
Other eruptions of similar size, such as the Paraná-Etendeka and Columbia River provinces, caused no mass extinction.
nodes.falsifier: High-resolution fossil records from several regions showing diversity steady right up to the boundary layer.

nodes.label: Mammals ate the dinosaurs' eggs
against: Dinosaurs and egg-eating mammals lived side by side for over 100 million years before the extinction.

nodes.label: End-Cretaceous mass extinction
nodes.text: About three quarters of species disappeared, including every dinosaur except birds.

edges.label: soot and sulfur fill the sky
edges.given: The impact released soot and sulfate in the amounts the models assume, and that much aerosol blocks most sunlight.
edges.note: Valid if the premise holds. The premise is the uncertain part, so the arrow is faint despite being a deduction.

edges.label: no light for plants or plankton
edges.given: The darkness lasted longer than most plankton and plants survive without light.

edges.label: food chains fail
edges.note: The best explanation of who survived: animals that did not depend on fresh plant growth. Rival: a slow decline from volcanic warming, which would not favour them this sharply.

edges.label: warming and acid pulses
edges.note: Generalised from the cases on the target box: two extinctions that line up with huge eruptions, and large eruptions that caused none.

edges.label: made the blow worse
edges.note: If real, it amplified the impact rather than causing a separate extinction.
